connections.description: Two circumpolar hunting peoples with the same answer: the dead keep a village of their own alongside this one, doing what they always did, with the boundary open in both directions to whoever knows how to cross it.
Both put the other world inside the landscape — under the mound, under the lake — rather than above the sky, and both make it a place a living specialist can enter and come back from.
Both keep the dead close and negotiable rather than judged, and both were documented largely through the categories of an incoming religion that reorganized what it recorded.

Two Indigenous traditions whose written record was made by outsiders during active suppression, and in both the specialist’s journey on behalf of a sick person is the working core rather than the doctrine about where the dead go.

Neighbours across the same forests answering the same question in opposite directions: the Finnic dead are ferried over a black river into a grey country where nothing distinguishes anyone, while the Sámi dead are a short way underfoot, warm, herding, and still doing business with the living.

name: Cārvāka (Lokāyata)
description: India’s materialist school denied the whole apparatus from inside the Indian conversation: no soul separable from the body, no karma, no rebirth, no heaven, no hell, no liberation. Consciousness arises from the elements as intoxication arises from mixed ingredients, and ends when they disperse. Its most quoted line advises borrowing to drink ghee, since the body once burned does not return. Almost nothing of its literature survives — it is known mostly through opponents quoting it in order to refute it.
essay:
Every framework in this atlas that denies an afterlife does so from outside the traditions that assert one. Cārvāka is the exception: a school that argued the case in Sanskrit, inside Indian philosophy, against Vedic ritualists and Buddhists and Jains simultaneously, and was taken seriously enough that the major schools felt obliged to answer it for well over a thousand years.

Its positions are austere. Only the four gross elements — earth, water, fire, air — are real; ether is rejected because it cannot be perceived. Only perception is a reliable means of knowledge, and inference, which is how everyone else gets to invisible souls and unseen karmic mechanisms, is unreliable because it always smuggles in an unverified general premise. There is no ātman distinct from the body. Consciousness is a property that emerges when the elements are combined in a living body, as the intoxicating power emerges when certain ingredients are mixed although none of them is intoxicating alone — an analogy the opponents quote constantly, and one that is recognizably a claim about emergence. When the body dies the combination ends and consciousness ends with it. There is therefore no rebirth, no karmic ledger carrying forward, no svarga and no naraka, and no mokṣa, since there is no bondage of the kind the other schools describe.

What follows is a critique of religion as economics. The Vedic rituals do not deliver their promised results; the priests who perform them eat well; and if an animal sacrificed at a rite really went to heaven, the school asked, why does the sacrificer not offer his own father? The famous verse attributed to Bṛhaspati advises that while life is yours, live joyfully, and that nobody escapes death — and adds, with deliberate provocation, that one should borrow money to drink ghee, since the body once burned does not return. Read as hedonism that is thin. Read as an argument, it is the point being made in its rudest available form: the debt cannot be collected from someone who does not exist.

The school's literature is essentially lost. The Bṛhaspati Sūtra survives only in fragments quoted by opponents, and the fullest presentation is the opening chapter of Mādhava's fourteenth-century Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha — which sets Cārvāka out first precisely as the position to be demolished before the real work begins. Almost everything known is therefore filtered through people arguing against it, which means the hedonism may be caricature and the epistemology may be the serious part.

It belongs in the atlas because it demonstrates that the Indian traditions' shared premises were contested at home, by Indians, with arguments. The wheel of rebirth is not what everyone in India believed. It is what most of them believed, over the objections of people who said the whole structure rested on an inference nobody could check.
story: The debate has been running since morning and the Naiyāyika has just finished a long, elegant demonstration that the self must persist, since memory requires a rememberer. The materialist waits, and then asks him one question: whether he has ever perceived such a self, or only inferred one. The Naiyāyika says inference is a valid means of knowledge. The materialist agrees that it works splendidly for smoke and fire, where anyone may go and check. Then he asks who has gone and checked the other world, and come back, and reported. The hall is quiet. Somebody at the edge, a young man who has been taught since childhood that his conduct is being recorded, finds that his hands are cold, and that he is not sure whether what he feels is horror at the impiety or something much more like being let out of a room.

primaryDoctrine: Only the four perceptible elements — earth, water, fire and air — are real; ether is rejected as imperceptible. Perception is the sole reliable means of knowledge, and inference is unreliable because it rests on an unverifiable general premise, which is precisely how the other schools reach souls and karma. There is no ātman distinct from the body: consciousness emerges when the elements are combined in a living body, as intoxicating power emerges from ingredients none of which is intoxicating alone, and ceases when the combination ends. There is therefore no rebirth, no karmic carry-forward, no svarga, no naraka, and no mokṣa, since there is no bondage of the kind assumed. Vedic ritual is criticized as an economy benefiting its priests — if the sacrificed animal reaches heaven, why not sacrifice one’s own father? The verse attributed to Bṛhaspati advises living joyfully while life lasts, since the body once burned does not return. The literature survives almost entirely in hostile quotation, chiefly Mādhava’s Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, so the hedonism may be caricature and the epistemology the serious core.

metadata.structuralTaxonomy: Death → the elemental combination dissolves → consciousness, being a property of that combination, ends with it → no soul departs, no karma carries forward, no realm receives anything, and no liberation is required because no bondage was ever demonstrated.

connections.description: The same conclusion reached independently in Greece and India within a century or two of each other, and by much the same route: nothing survives, the fear is misplaced, and the argument is aimed at priests as much as at metaphysics.

The house opposition. Cārvāka denies precisely what the Purāṇic system elaborates — ātman, karma, the fourteen lokas, rebirth and mokṣa — and does it in Sanskrit, from inside, on the grounds that none of it has ever been perceived.

Buddhism denies a permanent self and keeps rebirth and karmic consequence; Cārvāka denies the self and takes rebirth down with it — which is why Buddhist logicians spent centuries arguing that consciousness cannot be a product of the elements.

Against a cosmos where karma is literal matter adhering to the soul and liberation means shedding every particle of it, Cārvāka answers that there is no soul for anything to adhere to and no one to be liberated.
